# Atherothrombotic Outcomes After Sodium‐Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors Versus Dipeptidyl Peptidase‐4 Inhibitors in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes: A Territory‐Wide Retrospective Cohort Study

**Authors:** Pauline Yeung Ng; Andrew Kei‐Yan Ng; April Ip; Wai Ching Sin; Kai‐Hang Yiu

**Affiliations:** 1 Department of Adult Intensive Care, Queen Mary Hospital, Hong Kong, SAR, China | 2 Critical Care Medicine Unit, School of Clinical Medicine, Li Ka Shing Faculty of Medicine, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, SAR, China | 3 Department of Medicine, Queen Mary Hospital, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, SAR, China | 4 Division of Cardiology, Department of Medicine, The University of Hong Kong‐Shenzhen Hospital, Shen Zhen, China

## Abstract

This study compared the risks of atherothrombotic major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with type 2 diabetes taking SGLT2 (sodium‐glucose cotransporter 2) inhibitors to those taking DPP‐4 (dipeptidyl peptidase‐4) inhibitors.

All adult patients (≥18 years of age) with type 2 diabetes and newly prescribed with SGLT2 inhibitors or DPP‐4 inhibitors across all public hospitals in Hong Kong between January 2015 and December 2019 were included. Patients were propensity matched in a 1:1 ratio using a caliper distance of 0.2 without replacement. The primary outcome was atherothrombotic major adverse cardiovascular events as a composite outcome of cardiovascular mortality, nonfatal stroke, and nonfatal myocardial infarction. Time‐to‐first event analysis was conducted using a univariable Cox proportional hazards model. Primary and secondary analyses were repeated using stabilized inverse probability weighting and propensity score adjustment in the complete case cohort. A total of 20 642 patients (10 321 SGLT2 inhibitors versus 10 321 DPP‐4 inhibitors) were included in the final analysis. The mean age was 59±11 years, and 13 142 (63.7%) were men. The median follow‐up period was 2.9 years. The use of SGLT2 inhibitors was associated with a significant reduction in atherothrombotic major adverse cardiovascular events (453 [4.4%] versus 719 [7.0%]; hazard ratio, 0.64 [95% CI, 0.57–0.72]; P<0.001) compared with DPP‐4 inhibitors. SGLT2 inhibitors were independently associated with reduced all‐cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, stroke, myocardial infarction, and incident dialysis (all P values <0.001).

SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with diabetes were independently associated with reduction in atherothrombotic major adverse cardiovascular events, all‐cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, and incident dialysis, compared with DPP‐4 inhibitors.

Keywords: cardiovascular mortality, DPP‐4 inhibitor, myocardial infarction, SGLT2 inhibitor, type 2 diabetes

Subject Categories: Thrombosis, Coronary Artery Disease, Cerebrovascular Disease/Stroke

## What Is New?

- In addition to the known benefits to cardiovascular outcomes and mortality, we showed that SGLT2 (sodium‐glucose cotransporter 2) inhibitors are associated with a lower risk of myocardial infarction and stroke compared with DPP‐4 (dipeptidyl peptidase‐4) inhibitors.

## What Are the Clinical Implications?

- The underlying risk of atherothrombotic outcomes should be considered when clinicians are faced with the decision to prescribe add‐on oral hypoglycemic agents.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have shown that SGLT2 (sodium‐glucose cotransporter 2) inhibitors reduce the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and adverse renal events among patients with type 2 diabetes. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 However, the reductions in MACE were mainly driven by reduction in hospitalization for heart failure, whereas the effects on atherothrombotic MACE, including cardiovascular mortality, nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), and nonfatal stroke, were less clear. A meta‐analysis of the 6 largest RCTs showed that SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the hazard for MACE (hazard ratio [HR], 0.90), but data for individual components of MI or stroke were not examined. 7 In another meta‐analysis of 53 RCTs with 88 390 participants using Bayesian analysis, SGLT2 inhibitors were associated with a reduction in mortality but not MI or stroke. 8 One systemic review and meta‐analysis of 3 RCTs with 34 322 participants concluded that benefits in reducing atherothrombotic MACE were only confined to patients with established cardiovascular disease. 9

Most RCTs used a new‐user design and recruited patients with relatively stabilized diabetic control during run‐in periods. Given the common real‐world scenario of SGLT2 inhibitors initiation during a period of highly dynamic management of type 2 diabetes with frequent concurrent use of other antidiabetic agents, such new‐user designs can significantly diminish the generalizability or even validity of study results. 10 Moreover, data focusing on atherothrombotic MACE, such as stroke outcomes, are sparse. Only the Effect of Sotagliflozin on Cardiovascular and Renal Events in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes and Moderate Renal Impairment Who Are at Cardiovascular Risk (SCORED) trial showed that sotagliflozin reduced the risk of stroke as a post hoc end point. 6 In a pooled analysis of 5 RCTs including 46 969 participants, SGLT2 inhibitors were associated with 50% reduction of hemorrhagic stroke, with a neutral effect on total stroke risk (relative risk, 0.49; P=0.007). 11 All studies had compared SGLT2 inhibitors to placebo, lending uncertainty around their effects compared with other diabetic drugs, which would inform decision making in the clinical setting.

In this study, the risks of atherothrombotic MACE, including MI, stroke, and incident dialysis associated with SGLT2 inhibitors were compared with DPP‐4 (dipeptidyl peptidase‐4) inhibitors among people with type 2 diabetes from a territory‐wide cohort in Hong Kong. We hypothesized that SGLT2 inhibitors are associated with a reduction in atherothrombotic MACE and renal events.

## METHODS

The data that support the findings of this study are available from P.Y.N. (pyeungng@hku.hk) upon reasonable request.

### Study Design and Population

Data on new users of SGLT2 inhibitors or DPP‐4 inhibitors between January 1, 2015 and December 31, 2019, from all public hospitals in Hong Kong, were reviewed. Patients' baseline characteristics, clinical information, and outcomes were retrieved from the Clinical Data and Analysis Reporting System of the Hospital Authority in Hong Kong. Adult patients (≥18 years of age) with type 2 diabetes who received SGLT2 inhibitors or DPP‐4 inhibitors for the first time or had not received these drugs within 12 months before the index date were included. Type 2 diabetes was defined as having an International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD‐9‐CM) code starting with 250, except those indicating type 1 diabetes, or having baseline hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) ≥6.5%, or using any antidiabetic medications (ie, insulins, GLP‐1 [glucagon‐like peptide‐1] agonists, or oral hypoglycemic agents). During the recruitment period, GLP‐1 agonists were licensed only for treatment of type 2 diabetes in this locality. Patients who received SGLT2 inhibitors or DPP‐4 inhibitors for other indications and did not have diabetes were not included. Exclusion criteria were patients with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <25 mL/min per 1.73 m2, or patients who were started on both SGLT2 inhibitors and DPP‐4 inhibitors on the index date, or patients who were started on SGLT2 inhibitors or DPP‐4 inhibitors during hospitalization but were not yet discharged at the end of the study period. This study was conducted in accordance with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki of 1975 and its later amendments and was approved by the institutional review board of the University of Hong Kong/Hospital Authority Hong Kong West Cluster with a waiver of signed informed consent (institutional review board reference number: UW 22‐561) on July 28, 2022.

### Definitions of Exposures

We defined the index date as the first date of dispensing SGLT2 inhibitors or DPP‐4 inhibitors. SGLT2 inhibitors included canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin. DPP‐4 inhibitors included alogliptin, linagliptin, linagliptin/metformin, saxagliptin, sitagliptin, and vildagliptin. Patients were assigned to either the SGLT2 inhibitors group or DPP‐4 inhibitors group and followed up according to their assigned drug group. Patients who were prescribed medication from the alternative drug group were censored on the dispense date of the alternative drug.

### Definitions of Study Outcomes

The primary outcome was atherothrombotic MACE as a composite outcome of cardiovascular mortality, nonfatal stroke, and nonfatal MI. Secondary outcomes included all‐cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, MI, stroke, incident dialysis, and unplanned coronary revascularization. Unplanned coronary revascularization was defined as coronary artery bypass graft surgery or percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) performed for MI or unstable angina. The study outcomes, including MI, stroke, dialysis, and coronary artery bypass graft surgery, were defined by ICD‐9‐CM codes listed in Data S1. PCI was defined by ICD‐9‐CM codes and the Hong Kong PCI registry. Death was defined by the death registry of Hong Kong, and the cause of death was recorded in the death registry. All outcome events were recorded until the date of death, or the data cutoff date of March 31, 2022, whichever occurred first.

### Definitions of Covariates

Patients' baseline characteristics including age, sex, HbA1c, eGFR, duration of diabetes, and comorbidities were collected. All comorbidities were considered before the index date, and detailed ICD‐9‐CM codes, including for atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter, cerebrovascular diseases, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease, hypertension, and malignancy are listed in Data S1. The use of concomitant cardiovascular medications, including metformin, insulin, statins, β‐blockers, angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitors, and angiotensin receptor blockers were recorded. Baseline laboratory results were defined as results closest to the index date.

### Statistical Analysis

All analyses were performed with prespecified outcomes and statistical methods. Categorical variables were described as frequency with percentage and continuous variables as mean±SD or median with interquartile range. Categorical variables were compared with Fisher exact test or Pearson χ2 test, as appropriate. Continuous variables were compared using the Student t test or Mann‐Whitney U test. A logistic regression model was constructed to predict the likelihood of receiving an SGLT2 inhibitor or DPP‐4 inhibitor. All predictors were selected a priori based on biological plausibility, including age, sex, baseline HbA1c, duration of diabetes, baseline eGFR, and comorbidities such as history of atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter, cerebrovascular diseases, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, congestive heart failure, coronary artery diseases, hypertension, previous PCI or coronary artery bypass graft surgery, and malignancies. The use of metformin, insulin, angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, β‐blockers, statins, and ezetimibe, and the calendar year of index medication initiation were also considered. These variables are the same as those listed in Table 1 and were all included in the propensity score match model. Propensity score matching was then performed using a 1:1 matching ratio with nearest neighbor and sampling with no replacement with a caliper of 0.2 times the SD of the logit of the propensity scores. A univariable Cox proportional hazards model was used to evaluate the relationship between the use of SGLT2 inhibitors or DPP‐4 inhibitors and clinical outcomes in a time‐to‐first‐event analysis. In models where the outcome did not include mortality, death was considered as a competing event.

To ensure stringent control for confounders, the association between the use of SGLT2 inhibitors or DPP‐4 inhibitors and both primary and secondary outcomes were examined again using stabilized inverse probability weighting with robust estimators of standard error and propensity score adjustment in the complete case cohort. The equation for stabilized inverse probability weighting is explained in Data S2.

### Sensitivity Analysis

First, a multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression was performed, adjusting for the same covariates mentioned above, to examine the association between the exposure and the primary outcome using all complete cases before propensity score matching. Second, multiple imputations by chained equation were used to handle missing data in the entire cohort. Following imputation, multivariable Cox regression analysis was repeated to test the robustness of our findings. Third, the E value was computed to assess the potential effect of unmeasured confounding. 12 Finally, falsification testing was performed using cholecystectomy and senile cataract as falsification outcomes because they were biologically implausible to be related to the exposure of interest.

### Subgroup Analysis

Subgroup analyses on the outcome of atherothrombotic MACE was performed according to the following dichotomized subgroups: preexisting cardiovascular disease, HbA1c >8%, duration of diabetes >7 years, age >60 years, sex, and baseline creatinine ≤60 mL/min per 1.73 m2. Preexisting cardiovascular disease was defined by any of the following: coronary artery disease, previous PCI, previous coronary artery bypass graft surgery, and cerebrovascular diseases.

All analyses were performed using Stata MP software, version 16.1 (StataCorp, College Station, TX). A 2‐tailed P value of <0.007 was considered statistically significant, because we applied the Bonferroni correction by dividing the common threshold of 0.05 by the 7 primary and secondary outcomes.

## RESULTS

### Patient Characteristics

A total of 73 111 patients with diabetes were considered for inclusion between January 2015 and December 2019. After excluding 4061 (5.6%) patients due to application of exclusion criteria, and 6674 (9.1%) patients due to missing values in any of the variables used in the propensity score matching model, a total of 62 376 patients were included in the complete case cohort, including 10 321 (16.5%) users of SGLT2 inhibitors and 52 055 (83.5%) users of DPP‐4 inhibitors. After 1:1 propensity score matching, a total of 10 321 users of SGLT2 inhibitors and 10 321 users of DPP‐4 inhibitors were included in the final analysis, representing 33.1% of the complete case cohort (Figure 1). There were 2443 (11.8%) patients who had index drugs prescribed during hospitalization and 18 199 (88.2%) patients who had index drugs prescribed as outpatients. The mean age of the cohort was 59±11 years, and 13 142 (63.7%) were men. Baseline characteristics and medication use of the propensity score matched cohort and the stabilized inverse probability weighted cohort are shown in Tables 1 and 2, respectively. Baseline characteristics of patients in the complete case cohort are shown in Table S1, and baseline hypoglycemic medications usage is presented in Table S2. All variables in Table 1 were included in the propensity score model and were well‐balanced between groups with standardized differences <0.1.

### Primary Outcome: Atherothrombotic MACE

A total of 453 patients (4.4%) in the SGLT2 inhibitor group and 719 patients (7.0%) in the DPP‐4 inhibitor group developed the primary outcome of atherothrombotic MACE during the median of 2.9 (2.3–4.0) years of follow‐up. The risk of MACE was lower in SGLT2 inhibitors users compared with DPP‐4 inhibitors users (HR, 0.64 [95% CI, 0.57–0.72]; P<0.001), translating to an absolute between‐group difference of 2.6 percentage points (95% CI, 1.9–3.2) and a number needed to treat of 38. Detailed results are presented in Table 3 and Figure 2.

### Secondary Outcomes

All‐cause mortality occurred in 315 patients (3.1%) in the SGLT2 inhibitor group and 755 patients (7.3%) in the DPP‐4 inhibitor group. The risk of all‐cause mortality was lower in SGLT2 inhibitors users compared with DPP‐4 inhibitors users (HR, 0.44 [95% CI, 0.38–0.50]; P<0.001). Cardiovascular mortality was lower in SGLT2 inhibitors users compared with DPP‐4 inhibitors users (105 [1.0%] versus 206 [2.0%]; HR, 0.53 [95% CI, 0.42–0.67]; P<0.001). The risk of nonfatal stroke was lower in SGLT2 inhibitors users (251 [2.4%] versus 362 [3.5%]; HR 0.71, [95% CI, 0.60–0.83]; P<0.001), as was the risk of nonfatal MI (154 [1.5%] versus 272 [2.6%]; HR, 0.58 [95% CI, 0.48–0.71]; P<0.001) and incident dialysis (43 [0.4%] versus 155 [1.5%]; HR, 0.29 [95% CI, 0.21–0.40]; P<0.001). The risk of unplanned coronary revascularization was similar between the 2 groups (130 [1.3%] versus 153 [1.5%]; HR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.69–1.11]; P=0.27). These results remained the same after using stabilized inverse probability weighting and propensity score adjustment (P<0.001 for MACE and all secondary outcomes except unplanned coronary revascularization). Detailed results are presented in Table 3 and Figure 3.

### Sensitivity Analyses

In the complete case cohort, the risk of MACE was lower in SGLT2 inhibitors users compared with DPP‐4 inhibitors users after adjustment in multivariable Cox proportional hazards model (adjusted HR, 0.72 [95% CI, 0.65–0.80]; P<0.001) (Table S3). The results for secondary outcomes were also consistent. Only 2 variables in the propensity score model, baseline HbA1c and eGFR, had missing data. Multiple imputation was conducted, and the imputed cohort included all 6674 patients (9.7%) who were excluded due to missing values in any of the variables used in the propensity score model. The association between SGLT2 inhibitors and decreased risk of MACE in the imputed data set remained significant (adjusted HR, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.66–0.81]; P<0.001), as was the association with all secondary outcomes except unplanned coronary revascularization (Table S3). The E value for the hazard ratio for the primary outcome of atherothrombotic MACE was 2.06. Finally, falsification testing showed that SGLT2 inhibitors were not associated with differences in the clinical outcomes of cholecystectomy and senile cataract compared with DPP‐4 inhibitors (Table S3).

### Subgroup Analysis

The effect of SGLT2 inhibitors on the occurrence of MACE was modified by the duration of diabetes and baseline creatinine clearance. The benefit of SGLT2 inhibitors on MACE was greater in patients who had duration of diabetes >7 years compared with ≤7 years (HR, 0.57 versus HR, 0.73; P for interaction=0.035) and greater in patients with baseline eGFR ≤60 compared with >60 (HR, 0.57 versus HR, 0.76; P for interaction=0.019). The presence of previous cardiovascular disease, diabetic control (HbA1c >8%), age, and sex did not modify the association between SGLT2 inhibitors and MACE (Table S4 and Figure S1).

## DISCUSSION

In this cohort of 62 376 adult patients with type 2 diabetes and over a median follow‐up of 3.4 years, the use of SGLT2 inhibitors were associated with lower risks of atherothrombotic MACE, compared with the use of DPP‐4 inhibitors. We provide robust data to support the cerebrovascular and cardiovascular benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors, beyond commonly reported anti‐heart failure effects. The risks of stroke, MI, cardiovascular mortality, all‐cause mortality, and incident dialysis were all lower in the SGLT2 inhibitors group, with an exaggerated benefit in patients with long‐standing diabetes >7 years. The broad spectrum of benefits on atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease of SGLT2 inhibitors over DPP‐4 inhibitors will help to inform the choice during escalation of antidiabetic therapy, offering practicable data in addition to comparison with placebo in RCTs.

We focused on the atherothrombotic events of stroke and MI in our study and showed that SGLT2 inhibitors have beneficial effects, with 30% to 40% reduction in hazards compared with DPP‐4 inhibitors. This pharmacological advantage was more variable in previous RCTs that mostly compared against placebo. 1 , 2 , 3 , 6 , 7 For example, in the Empagliflozin Cardiovascular Outcome Event Trial in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Patients–Removing Excess Glucose (EMPA‐REG OUTCOME) trial, the primary end point of atherothrombotic MACE was reduced by 14%, but only driven by reduction in cardiovascular death but not nonfatal stroke or nonfatal MI. 1 A pooled analysis of 10 RCTs including 71 553 participants with a median follow‐up of 2.3 years showed no significant protection against acute MI. 13 Another Bayesian meta‐analysis of 53 RCTs and 88 390 participants showed no significant reduction in incidence of stroke, but a weak benefit in reducing acute MI. 8 All of these RCTs compared the efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitors against placebo, and the benefits over other second‐line antidiabetic medication remain unclear. In our study, the event curves for acute MI and stroke diverged between groups after 1 to 2 years of follow‐up. It is likely that the protective effects of SGLT2 inhibitors on atherosclerosis only emerge after an extended period of drug use and are detectable in a larger cohort with a median of 2.9 years of follow‐up. Importantly, this benefit was observed in a cohort of patients with diabetes regardless of established cardiovascular disease, lending evidence to extend the recommendations for SGLT2 inhibitors to all patients at risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease independent of glucose control. This strategy is in line with major guidelines for diabetic management to target the equally important but distinct pathways of glycemic control and mitigating cardiovascular risk. 14 , 15

Although the benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors on heart failure and kidney outcomes have been firmly established, the mechanisms on cerebrovascular and coronary protection remain a subject of ongoing interest. Emerging evidence supports the anti‐inflammatory effects of SGLT2 inhibitors in downregulating serum inflammatory molecules such as NLRP3 (NLR family pyrin domain containing 3) inflammasome, caspase‐1, and interleukin‐1ß after 1 year of use in patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. 16 This translated to more stable fibrous cap and less lipid deposition measurable by optical coherence tomography of the coronary arteries. The mechanistic benefits on cerebrovascular outcomes of ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke are less well understood, with data from meta‐analysis suggesting protective effects on hemorrhagic subtypes only. 11 Recent real‐world data, including patients with concomitant diabetes and atrial fibrillation, showed a modest hazard in risk of ischemic stroke (HR, 1.12) and strong hazard of intracranial hemorrhage (HR, 1.57) in nonusers of SGLT2 inhibitors. 17 It is possible that cerebrovascular benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors are modulated by suppression of the mammalian target of rapamycin signaling pathway and downstream cerebral amyloid deposition. 18

The practical implications of our data in comparing 2 strategies in escalation of diabetic medication, SGLT2 inhibitors, and DPP‐4 inhibitors provide evidence to strongly recommend prioritizing prescription of SGLT2 inhibitors for their benefits over a broad range of atherosclerotic MACE, kidney, and mortality outcomes. The significant reduction in all‐cause mortality (HR, 0.44) and cardiovascular mortality (HR, 0.53) regardless of underlying established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease were confirmatory of findings from large RCTs and meta‐analyses. 8 , 13 , 19 In terms of renal outcomes, previous cohorts, including patients with mean eGFR of 90 mL/min per 1.73 m2, demonstrated halving of renal events over a mean follow‐up of 14.9 months. Our observation period, which was longer for a cohort with lower median eGFR of 81 mL/min per 1.73 m2, resulted in stronger renoprotective effects of 70% reduction in incident dialysis, highlighting the accretive benefits of long‐term SGLT2 inhibitor use.

The use of an active comparator in this study offered insights to the efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitors in real‐world practice, resembling the typical decision bifurcation faced by practicing clinicians. The incident new user design minimized biases and the risk of residual confounding compared with studies of prevalent users. 20 Our findings were in line with trends from RCTs and supported by biological plausibility and falsification outcomes. Notwithstanding, the observational nature of the study restricted analysis by prescription data, and we could not ascertain drug adherence. It is possible that premature termination of medication was underrecognized but should likely bias the effect toward the null. Most clinical outcomes were adjudicated by diagnostic codes, and it was not possible to understand differences in the disease severity of nonfatal stroke or nonfatal MI. Last, because patients who crossed over to the other drug class were censored at the time of crossover, the effects of dual prescriptions could not be examined.

In conclusion, we showed that SGLT2 inhibitors were independently associated with reduction in atherothrombotic MACE, including stroke and MI, in a real‐world setting compared with an active comparator of DPP‐4 inhibitors. There is strong evidence to prioritize early initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, in the absence of compelling contraindications. Future observational studies should aim to elucidate the efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitors as first‐ or second‐line agents in diabetic management.
